sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** No.
   - **Where:** The H1 "River ferry timetable" (about x 120–480, y 75–115) sits over three small paragraphs of prose (about x 120–222, y 140–196). Nothing visible on the page is a timetable: no departure times, no table, no stops, no days. Below y ≈ 200 the frame is empty white down to y 800.
   - **What the viewer meets:** A passenger comes for one thing, the next sailing. The heading promises it, the page doesn't deliver it, and they're left wondering whether the page is broken or the times are hidden in the paragraphs. Times written as running prose in text this small would force them to read every sentence just to find one departure.
   - **Why:** WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6 Headings and Labels says a heading must describe what its section holds. Here it describes content that isn't there.
   - **Fix:** Either put the actual timetable under the heading (departures by stop and day, in a table the eye can scan), or rename the heading to match what the section really is, such as "About the river ferry", with the timetable following it. If a table is meant to sit in the empty space and failed to render or load, the heading is fine once it appears. Check the live page.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect. Major: this decides whether the page does its job at all.

**What's working.** The heading is the clear landing point: bold, dark, much bigger than anything else, and in plain words, so a first-time viewer knows in one second what the page claims to be. The plain black-on-white sans styling suits a public utility page and adds no ornament that would compete with the information.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Copy finished?** I couldn't check whether the copy is finished, meaning free of placeholder text and typos. The paragraphs are too small to read at this resolution, and I couldn't open a zoomed crop because the crop command was refused. They look like real sentences about the service. Proofread them at full size.
- **Missing timetable?** The empty lower three quarters of the page may be a capture taken before a timetable loaded. Check in a live browser whether a table or widget is supposed to appear there.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 1 no (each heading names what its section holds), 1 unsure (copy finished, with no placeholder text and no spelling mistakes)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

All three lines pass, but only narrowly, and the director should know why. The title "River ferry timetable" (about x 120–480, y 75–112) dominates easily, and the body text is clearly a different level. The trouble is that the body text (three short paragraphs at x 120–222, y 140–196) is so small it looks like 3–4 px type on a 1280×800 image. At a glance it reads as fine print, not as body text the viewer is meant to read. The two levels don't collide, which is all this section asks about. The real defect is that the body text can't be read, and that belongs under the Text section's question on body size. Another critic should also flag that a page titled "timetable" shows no timetable at all.

**What's working.**
- The title is the one clear entry point. It is bold, dark and roughly ten times the body size, alone in open space at the top left, so the eye knows where to start.
- The title and body differ in weight as well as size: a heavy bold title over regular-weight text. The levels separate by more than size alone, as Dair recommends in *Design with Type*, chapters 8a to 8g.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was denied in this session, so I judged from the whole image at 1280×800. The image is one screen tall, so this is unlikely to have hidden anything.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** No. The 1280×800 frame holds two things: the headline at about x 120–480, y 75–115, and a narrow block of three tiny paragraphs at about x 120–222, y 140–197. Everything right of x≈480 and below y≈200 is blank, which is roughly 90% of the frame. It is one gathered area, but nothing shapes it or plays against it, so it doesn't read as a choice. It reads as a page whose content is missing, and a page titled "timetable" shows no timetable at all. Ruder's printed–unprinted tension needs a dense area to set against the open one, and here the only dense area is a 100 px column of text that is too small to read. If the table didn't load or sits below the fold, the capture explains it: check in a live browser that the timetable renders in this first screen. If this is the page as designed, the fix is to give the content area its job. Put the timetable in the frame, and let the body text and table take a column width related to the headline, so the open space becomes the margin around a real block (Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts" and "Form and counter-form"). Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the visual weight is the bold headline plus the grey speck of body text, packed into the top-left corner above y≈200. The right side and the bottom 600 px carry nothing to balance it, so the page looks unfinished and tips up and to the left. Arnheim locates weight in size, darkness and isolation, and a heavy side needs a counterweight. The fix is the same as in finding 1: once real content (the timetable) fills the area below and to the right, it acts as the counterweight. Moving the two existing elements around won't fix this (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Defect. Weight: major. This is the same problem as finding 1.
3. **Does the arrangement lead the eye from the first element through the rest, with no line, gaze, or pointing shape that leads it off the edge?** No. The eye lands on "River ferry timetable", drops to the tiny paragraphs at y≈140, and the path stops at y≈197. There is no next element. A reader who came for departure times never reaches any, and gets no cue that there is more below. The fix is to place the timetable directly under the intro so the path runs headline → intro → times. If the table is meant to sit below the fold, the first screen needs something that shows it continues. I judged this by common sense; I didn't open an entry for it. Defect. Weight: major. Same problem as findings 1 and 2.

**What's working.** The headline and the intro text share one clean left edge at x≈120, with a generous top-left margin. That edge is the one structural line on the page, and the timetable should hang from it too. The headline sits about 30 px above its intro, so it clearly belongs to the text it introduces.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I can't tell whether the blank area is the design or a timetable that hadn't loaded or rendered yet. Check the live page. I also couldn't run the crop script (Bash was refused), so I judged the small text block and edge alignment from the whole image only.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (empty space gathered and deliberate; visual weight balances; clear eye path)

sections.report:
I've finished the text walk and read the relevant entries. Only one line fails, and it's the one that decides this piece.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is body text large enough to read? No.** This covers the three intro paragraphs in a column about 100 px wide (x≈120–222, y≈140–196). Their cap height looks like 3–4 px, about one tenth of the 40 px heading "River ferry timetable" above them. At 1:1 no one can read the paragraphs, and even a full-resolution crop shows only grey bars of text. The viewer gets a title and a smudge, so whatever the paragraphs say about the service (they seem to cover crossing times and tide or weather delays) is lost. This is the one piece of content on the page, and it's what a ferry passenger came to read. At this size the regular weight also breaks up, so the dark text reads as mid-grey against the white. That's a symptom of the size, not a separate colour problem. Rule: body text is never smaller than the interface text around it, and Material 3 sets body text at 16 (Material Design 3 type scale, Body Large 16 against Label Large 14). Fix: set the paragraphs at normal reading size, about 16–18 px on screen. Widen the column so lines stay at about 45–75 characters at that size, which would be roughly 600–700 px here. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The heading is set well for display. It's one line in a bold grotesque, with spacing a little tighter than default and no awkward letter pairs, so it reads instantly as the title.
- The paragraphs are set flush left with a ragged right, separated by a little space and no indent. The structure is right, so the fix only needs a change of scale, not a reset.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the 3–4 px size is the design or the capture: for example, a page scaled down by a zoom or transform, or a text block caught mid-animation. Check in a live browser that the paragraphs' computed font size is not this small. If it isn't, the finding falls away.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (body text large enough), 0 unsure

First read: the eye lands on the bold near-black headline "River ferry timetable" at about (120–480, 75–115). It then drops to a column of very small paragraphs at (120–222, 140–196) and finds no timetable. The rest of the 1280×800 frame is empty white. I'm assuming this is a public web page that tells ferry riders when boats leave.

Walk, Color:
- Small palette: yes (near-black on white, no hue at all)
- Strong colour kept to a small share: yes (no saturated colour)
- Clear light-dark range that holds in grayscale: yes (dark headline and body on white)
- Warm forward, cool back: yes (no hues)
- Matching colours look the same: yes (one ink colour throughout)
- No vibrating edges: yes
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes (none used)
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes (nothing is colour-coded)
- Dark theme on dark gray: yes (light theme, does not apply)

No lines are `no` or `unsure`, so there are no reference entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is a single near-black ink on white with no hues, so every line passes.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The headline's near-black on white gives the strongest contrast the page can have, so in grayscale the structure is exactly what it is in colour. Because there's only one ink, no colour competes with the content.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photo, illustration, icon, logo or mark. It shows only a heading ("River ferry timetable") and three small paragraphs on a white page.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Everything below about y≈200 px is blank, and no timetable appears on a page titled "timetable". I can't see a broken-image icon or an empty placeholder box, so I can't tell whether an image or table failed to load or simply isn't there. Check in a live browser whether the timetable, a map or a picture should appear in that space.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
